title: Sharp low-degree Fourier weight of halfspaces
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal: For every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every linear threshold function \(f:\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}\), is \(\mathrm{W}^{\le 1}(f)=\hat\{f\}(\varnothing )^{2}+\sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat\{f\}(\{i\})^{2}\ge 2/\pi\)?
context:
The low-degree coefficients describe how much of a halfspace is visible through its mean and individual-coordinate correlations. The proposed lower bound holds across all dimensions and all weight vectors.

The source conjectures the bound \(2/\pi\), approached by odd-variable majority functions as dimension increases. The question is not a dimension-dependent numerical experiment.

De, Diakonikolas and Servedio give a lower bound strictly above \(1/2\) and an algorithm approximating the infimum over all halfspaces. Keeping only numerical approximation would weaken this already studied task, so the exact universal inequality is retained.

An August 2026 preprint claims the improved lower bound 0.53317, still below \(2/\pi\). Its proof has not been independently verified in this editorial review.
why: A sharp universal low-degree Fourier inequality for all halfspaces describes the spectral structure of a foundational Boolean function class.
status_note: The universal \(2/\pi\) inequality remains conjectural in the checked sources. The August 2026 preprint gives a claimed partial lower bound, not a resolution.

sentences: A halfspace is the sign of a weighted sum of input bits and a threshold.
Its degree-zero and degree-one Fourier coefficients measure its mean and coordinate correlations.
The question asks whether their squared weight is always at least \(2/\pi\).
Majority functions approach that proposed universal constant as dimension grows.
The exact inequality is retained because a general algorithm for merely approximating the extremal constant is already known.

definitions: A linear threshold function has \(f(x)=\operatorname{sign}(\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i} x_{i}- \theta )\) for some real weights \(w_{i}\) and threshold \(\theta\), with \(\operatorname{sign}(t)=1\) when \(t\ge 0\) and −1 otherwise. Constant functions are included. Under the uniform measure on \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}\), define \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum_{x} f(x)\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with empty product 1. Thus \(\hat\{f\}(\varnothing )\) is the mean and \(\hat\{f\}(\{i\})\) is the correlation with the i-th coordinate. The displayed squared coefficients are the Fourier weight in degrees zero and one. There is no bound on dimension, weights or bias, and no regularity assumption on the halfspace. The constant \(\pi\) is the usual circle constant.
answer_criterion: Prove the exact universal inequality or give a threshold function with a rigorous proof that its low-degree weight is strictly less than \(2/\pi\). Approximation of the extremal constant to 0.01 would not settle this universal proposition. An algorithm for approximating that constant is already known; the retained target is the source’s sharp inequality.
